title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 30
paragraphs: Returning to Gorki after seeing Prince Andrew, Pierre ordered his groom to have the horses ready and to wake him early in the morning, then immediately fell asleep behind a partition in a corner Boris had given up to him.
Before he was fully awake the next morning, everyone had already left the hut. The windowpanes were rattling and his groom was shaking him.
"Your excellency! Your excellency! Your excellency!" he kept repeating insistently while shaking Pierre by the shoulder without looking at him, apparently having lost all hope of waking him up.
"What? Has it begun? Is it time?" Pierre asked, waking up.
"Listen to the firing," said the groom, a discharged soldier. "All the gentlemen have gone out, and his Serene Highness himself rode past long ago."

Pierre dressed hastily and ran out to the porch. Outside everything was bright, fresh, dewy, and cheerful. The sun, just breaking through a cloud that had hidden it, shone with rays still half-blocked by clouds — over the roofs of the street opposite, the dew-spattered dust of the road, the walls of the houses, the windows, the fence, and Pierre's horses standing before the hut. The roar of guns sounded more clearly outside. An adjutant accompanied by a Cossack passed by at a brisk trot.
"It's time, Count; it's time!" cried the adjutant.

Telling the groom to follow him with the horses, Pierre walked down the street to the knoll from which he had surveyed the battlefield the day before. A crowd of military men had gathered there; staff members could be heard speaking in French, and Kutuzov's gray head in a white cap with a red band was visible, his gray neck sunk between his shoulders. He was looking through a field glass down the road ahead.

Climbing the steps to the knoll, Pierre looked at the scene before him, spellbound by its beauty. It was the same panorama he had admired from that spot the day before, but now the whole area was full of troops and covered by clouds of gun smoke, and the slanting rays of the bright sun, rising slightly to the left behind Pierre, cast penetrating streaks of rosy, golden-tinted light and long dark shadows across it all. The distant forest seemed carved from some precious yellowish-green stone; its undulating outline stood silhouetted against the horizon, pierced beyond Valuevo by the Smolensk road packed with troops. Closer by, golden cornfields glittered, interspersed with clusters of trees. Troops were visible everywhere — in front, to the right, and to the left. It was all vivid, majestic, and unexpected; but what struck Pierre most was the view of the battlefield itself — Borodino and the hollows on both sides of the Kolocha.

Above the Kolocha, at Borodino and on both sides of it — especially to the left where the Voyna River flows between its marshy banks into the Kolocha — a mist had spread that seemed to melt, dissolve, and become translucent as the brilliant sun appeared, magically coloring and defining everything. The gun smoke mingled with this mist, and across the whole expanse, through the haze, the morning sun's rays were reflected — flashing like lightning off the water, the dew, and the bayonets of troops massed along the riverbanks and in Borodino. A white church was visible through the mist, along with rooftops in Borodino, and dense masses of soldiers, green ammunition chests, and artillery pieces. And all of this moved — or seemed to move — as the smoke and mist spread over the entire space. Just as in the fog-filled hollow near Borodino, so along the entire line beyond it — and especially in the woods and fields to the left, in the valleys and on the hilltops — puffs of powder smoke kept springing up seemingly from nowhere, now individually, now in clusters, some translucent, others dense, swelling, growing, rolling, and merging, until they covered the whole panorama.
These puffs of smoke and — strange to say — the sound of the firing created the chief beauty of the scene.
"Puff!" — suddenly a round compact cloud of smoke appeared, shifting from violet to gray to milky white, and "boom!" came the report a second later.
"Puff! Puff!" — two clouds rose, pushing into each other and blending together; and "boom, boom!" came the sounds confirming what the eye had seen.

Pierre glanced back at the first cloud, which he'd seen as a round compact ball, and in its place floated balloons of smoke drifting to one side, and — "puff" (with a pause) — "puff, puff!" three and then four more appeared, and from each, at the same interval — "boom — boom, boom!" came fine, firm, precise sounds in reply. It seemed as though those smoke clouds sometimes raced and sometimes stood still while woods, fields, and glinting bayonets flew past them. From the left, across fields and bushes, large balls of smoke kept appearing followed by their solemn reports, while closer still, in the hollows and woods, small cloudlets burst from muskets — too quick to form full balls, but each with its own little echo. "Trakh-ta-ta-takh!" came the rapid crackle of musket fire, irregular and feeble compared to the cannon reports.

Pierre wanted to be there — amid that smoke, those gleaming bayonets, that movement and those sounds. He turned to look at Kutuzov and his staff, to compare his own impressions with theirs. They were all watching the battlefield as he was, and it seemed to him, with the same feelings. All their faces now shone with the latent warmth Pierre had noticed the day before and had fully understood after his conversation with Prince Andrew.
"Go, my dear fellow, go — and Christ be with you!" Kutuzov was saying to a general beside him, without taking his eye from the battlefield.
Having received this order, the general passed by Pierre on his way down the knoll.
"To the crossing!" the general said coldly and sternly in reply to a staff officer who asked where he was going.
"I'll go there too! I'm going too!" thought Pierre, and he followed the general.

The general mounted a horse a Cossack had brought him. Pierre went to his groom who was holding his horses and, asking which was the calmest, clambered onto it, grabbed it by the mane, and turning out his toes pressed his heels against its sides. Feeling his spectacles slipping off but unable to let go of the mane and reins, he galloped after the general — making the staff officers on the knoll smile as they watched him.
